explanations.explanation: Bildad says, "Show some sense, and then we can talk." (Job 18:2) That's the whole ask, and he puts it up front like a bouncer at the door. I think Job heard it as a pretty big "first." Bildad is Job's friend, and he starts with a push.

Bildad never says those words here. He says, "Show some sense, and then we can talk." (Job 18:2) A lot of folks expect the sin talk to come first, and it does show up later in his picture of the wicked. But his opening ask is about sense, not a confession.

Bildad doesn't give Job a waiting period. He says, "How long until you end these speeches? Show some sense, and then we can talk." (Job 18:2) No calendar, no days, just the ask for sense. I once waited years in a junk drawer for somebody to open it, and even I'd say that's a different kind of waiting.
Bildad asks, "Why are we regarded as cattle, as stupid in your sight?" (Job 18:3) So the word is stupid. I think that question stung him, and it seems to carry into the rest of his speech.

Lazy isn't the word Bildad uses. He asks, "Why are we regarded as cattle, as stupid in your sight?" (Job 18:3) The word is stupid, and Bildad is the one speaking. Nobody in this verse is calling anybody lazy.
Greedy never comes up here. Bildad says the friends are regarded "…as cattle, as stupid in your sight?" (Job 18:3) It's all about being seen as stupid. Nobody's guarding a cookie jar in this verse.

explanations.answer: The rocks moved from their place
explanations.explanation: Bildad asks, "…should the earth be forsaken on your account, or the rocks be moved from their place?" (Job 18:4) Two big questions, back to back. He's talking to Job, whom he calls someone who tears himself in anger. Rocks are about as stay-put as it gets, so I think he's making a point.

Rivers aren't in this verse. Bildad asks about the earth being forsaken and "…the rocks be moved from their place?" (Job 18:4) Dry rivers do sound dramatic, but the text keeps it to rocks. Good guess on the big-picture feel, though.

explanations.answer: The stars falling from the sky
explanations.explanation: No stars fall in this verse. Bildad asks whether "…the rocks be moved from their place?" (Job 18:4) Stars do light up my bakery sky, but Bildad stays on the ground with the rocks. The question is still a big one.

Bildad says, "…the lamp of the wicked is extinguished…" (Job 18:5) Then he says, "…the lamp beside him goes out." (Job 18:6) Same picture, said twice. A lamp that goes out leaves a tent dark, and that's the image he wants.

It's the opposite. Bildad says, "…the lamp of the wicked is extinguished; the flame of his fire does not glow." (Job 18:5) He's picturing a light that goes out, not one that never quits. My oven stays warm, but this lamp doesn't.

Stolen isn't the word here. Bildad says, "The light in his tent grows dark, and the lamp beside him goes out." (Job 18:6) The lamp goes out, and that's the picture he gives. A thief never shows up in these verses.

Look again at what Bildad says. "For his own feet lead him into a net, and he wanders into its mesh." (Job 18:8) No enemies are dragging anybody. It's his own feet doing the walking, which is a rough way to get caught.

Right, no enemies in this verse. Bildad says, "For his own feet lead him into a net, and he wanders into its mesh." (Job 18:8) His own feet take him there, and he wanders in. Bildad tells it as a man walking himself into trouble.

No safe place here. Bildad says, "Terrors frighten him on every side and harass his every step." (Job 18:11) Every side means there's no corner to rest in. I know a little about dark, cramped spots, and I can tell you worry has a way of following you in.
Right, it's False. Bildad says, "Terrors frighten him on every side and harass his every step." (Job 18:11) Every side, every step, no break. He pictures a man who can't find a calm spot anywhere.

Bildad says the wicked man "…is torn from the shelter of his tent and is marched off to the king of terrors." (Job 18:14) That's a heavy title, and it's the end of the road in his picture. I think this is one of his darkest lines.
Babylon isn't in this verse. Bildad says the man is "…marched off to the king of terrors." (Job 18:14) The king is named right there in the verse. It's a heavy line, and Babylon isn't part of it.
Egypt doesn't show up here. Bildad says he is "…marched off to the king of terrors." (Job 18:14) Pharaoh isn't mentioned anywhere in this speech. The verse calls him the king of terrors.
Roots is the first blank. Bildad says, "The roots beneath him dry up…" (Job 18:16) Roots are below the ground, out of sight. Bildad moves from fire to a picture of a plant.
Branches is the second blank. Bildad says, "…the branches above him wither away." (Job 18:16) Roots dry up below, and branches wither above. Both go in the same verse.
Waters isn't the word. Bildad says "The roots beneath him dry up…" (Job 18:16) Dry and water do go together, so I get the guess. But the text names roots.

Stones aren't in this verse. The text says "The roots beneath him dry up, and the branches above him wither away." (Job 18:16) Rocks did show up earlier in Bildad's speech (Job 18:4), but not here. Here it's all a withering tree.

No stars in this verse. Bildad says the "…roots beneath him dry up, and the branches above him wither away." (Job 18:16) He's looking at the ground and the tree, not the sky. My sky has the stars, and Bildad's picture here is a dying plant.
Yes. Bildad says, "The memory of him perishes from the earth, and he has no name in the land." (Job 18:17) Being forgotten is part of his picture. It's a sad line, and I think it hits hard.
It's True. Bildad says, "The memory of him perishes from the earth, and he has no name in the land." (Job 18:17) He pictures the wicked man being forgotten. That's a heavy thing to say about anyone.
It's the opposite. Bildad says, "He has no offspring or posterity among his people, no survivor where he once lived." (Job 18:19) No children to carry on a name. That's a very empty picture.

Right, it's False. Bildad says, "He has no offspring or posterity among his people, no survivor where he once lived." (Job 18:19) So no offspring or posterity among his people, and no survivor where he once lived. That's how he finishes the picture of the man's name fading out.

explanations.answer: One who does not know God
explanations.explanation: Bildad ends with, "Surely such is the dwelling of the wicked and the place of one who does not know God." (Job 18:21) That's his closing line. He ties the dwelling of the wicked to the one who does not know God.
Poor isn't the word. Bildad closes with "…the dwelling of the wicked and the place of one who does not know God." (Job 18:21) His final line is about the wicked and not knowing God, not money.

explanations.answer: One who has lost his flocks
explanations.explanation: Flocks aren't mentioned in this closing line. Bildad says it's "…the dwelling of the wicked and the place of one who does not know God." (Job 18:21) I know the sting of losing your place, but this verse isn't about animals. It ends on knowing God.
